Senses.Explanation: To pick out and bring forward is a public, transitive action in these records: something is selected or taken up and put where others can hear, see, inspect, or receive it. Zhenjing Kewen brings Mazu's Sun-Face Buddha and Moon-Face Buddha wording forward again for his audience (日面佛，月面佛，一一為君重拈出). Duanqiao Miaolun says he must bring out one phrase so that what heaven and humanity have not heard or seen may be heard and seen (拈出一句子，使天上人間未聞者聞、未見者見). Gaofeng Yuanmiao brings an old doubt forward again from the beginning in a letter (今日重疑，不免從頭拈出), and Lu Hang asks that the cases of the various houses not be brought forward before requesting one direct phrase (諸家因緣，不勞拈出). The same verb governs presented objects. Pufeng Haidong tells an unnamed monk who claims to have a jewel, “try bringing it out and let us see” (試拈出看). Baichi Yuan says he will take a bright pearl from inside his robe and present it before the assembly (不免乘時拈出，對眾分付). Tian'an Sheng and Yongji Rong bring out incense for public offering. These are not two different headword senses: phrases, cases, doubts, jewels, pearls, and incense are different direct objects of one selecting-and-presenting action. Chan bends that action into a standard verb for putting inherited cases and a participant's claimed answer into the public exchange, while retaining its use for objects physically displayed and offered.

Senses.Explanation: To take up an inherited case, encounter, or saying and bring it before listeners for comment. The action belongs to the public handling of the record: the material is raised, quoted, appraised, or deliberately left without further comment. Wumen Huikai's publication notice calls his book “forty-eight cases taking up and presenting the encounters of buddhas and ancestral teachers” (拈提佛祖機緣四十八則). Jingfu says lineage descendants successively raised and voiced the inherited material and took it up for comment (舉唱之、拈提之); his editorial rules classify the collected material as masters' “statements of taking up and commenting” (諸師拈提語). Yuanwu Keqin uses the verb for a person moving within and bringing forward the upward hinge (向箇裏出沒，向箇裏拈提). Dahui Zonggao puts two opposed statements together “without further taking them up for comment” (更無拈提), leaving students to distinguish them. Yulin Tongxiu says few in the communities had taken up and commented on the old woman's burning-the-hut case (者個公案叢林中少有拈提者). Dagui Huaixiu appraises Baofu Congzhan's handling as having considerable house style, then says that under questioning it again dragged through mud and carried water (保福拈提，頗有宗風，及乎問著，又却拖泥帶水). Senses.Explanation: The flower-lifting and smile scene names the paired actions attributed to the Buddha and Kashyapa; later masters quote, judge, and sometimes reject the scene’s inherited formulation. The flower-sermon scene: Shakyamuni Buddha holds up a flower before the Vulture Peak assembly, the assembly is at a loss, and Kashyapa smiles . The compact phrase joins two different actors' gestures; it does not say that one person both holds the flower and smiles. The recorded Buddha then entrusts Kashyapa with the treasury of the true teaching eye and a transmission outside teachings. Later masters challenge the scene. Yuelin Zongshan assigns thirty blows at the moment of the flower and smile. Dongshan Shouchu says people know the compact phrase but do not know the World-Honored One. Yulin Tongxiu calls it a single transmission and says it has made clear-eyed people laugh. Zhongfeng Mingben says that if the great affair were exhausted by such gestures, holding up the flower and smiling and cutting off an arm to settle the mind would be mere plays. Tianran Hanshi calls only this purport real and all other verbal teachings false, then immediately warns against making it a fixed reality. Zen defines the invoked Buddha and Kashyapa through this public scene, entrustment, and later examinations rather than through general hagiography.

Senses.Explanation: To take up incense is the ritual gesture that introduces the words or action attached to that incense in the particular ceremony. Konggu Daocheng takes up incense and names its recipient before saying it will be burned. Elsewhere an official, a disciple, or a named teacher takes it up before a question, dedication, lineage statement, or compact verdict. The gesture is stable; its actor, audience, recipient, and purpose are source-specific. It is therefore not defined as invariably public, dedicatory, or restricted to named teachers, and it remains distinct from subsequently burning the incense.

Senses.Explanation: A lantern is the monastery's visible light-holder, repeatedly bent into a public-stage object and impossible participant. Dizang points to one; an unnamed monk calls it form and asks which is mind; Guishan answers a question about the ancestral teacher by saying, 'A very good lantern.' Elsewhere it dozes while the exposed pillar is alert, dances while pillars knit their brows, is carried into the Buddha hall beneath the three gates, and exposes silent sitters. These literal, interrogated, and personified deployments still refer to the same lantern; the corpus supplies no hidden substance behind it.

Literally “lamp” and “record”: “lamp record.” The compound occurs 789 times in 91 allowlisted texts and names individual records and a family of titled compilations. Attested titles include the Jingde Transmission Lamp Record, Continued Transmission Lamp Record, Tiansheng Broad Lamp Record, and Jiatai Universal Lamp Record. Their headings and contents list masters, lineage heirs, and successive sections. A compiler’s rules says that after the Jingde collection, later compilations were named Continued Lamp, Linked Lamp, Universal Lamp, or Broad Lamp. An editorial preface says that damaged encounter wording and inaccurate comments were checked against the lamp records. These passages establish the title family, collective reference, and editorial use of the term; the entry does not assign the records a further function not stated by them.
Senses.Note: The headword-plus-transmission construction occurs 382 times in 61 texts; the headword-plus-continuation construction occurs 83 times in 13. Six apparent strings of the form “lamp record is...” are relative clauses about works or people listed in them, not self-definitions.
